title: Animals: A Tour of the Kingdoms

cards.h: A family of over a million
cards.b:
About 1.3 to 1.5 million animal species have been named, and most are insects. Knowing the main groups, and how each is built, shows how body plans evolved and why habitats matter for conservation.

Insects alone account for over half of all named species, and beetles are the most numerous group, a remark attributed to the biologist J.B.S. Haldane, who said that the Creator had 'an inordinate fondness for beetles'. India is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, with about 100,000 recorded animal species, including tigers, Asian elephants and the one-horned rhinoceros. Animals in turn pollinate plants, recycle matter and control pests.

Animals are multicellular eukaryotes that eat other organisms, have no cell walls, and most can move at some stage. They are grouped by body plan: symmetry, body layers, a body cavity, segmentation and a backbone.

The first animals appeared in the sea more than 600 million years ago. Most animals show bilateral symmetry, with left and right halves, which suits moving in one direction and goes along with a head end (cephalisation). Jellyfish and sea anemones have radial symmetry, like a wheel, and sponges have none. Animals also differ in whether the embryo has two or three tissue layers and whether there is a fluid-filled body cavity, the coelom. Animals take in food by eating, unlike plants, which make theirs.

• Porifera (sponges): pores, no true tissues.
  • Cnidaria: jellyfish, coral, stinging cells.
  • Platyhelminthes: flatworms, tapeworm.
  • Nematoda: roundworms.
  • Annelida: segmented worms like earthworms.
  • Mollusca: snails, octopus, soft body.
  • Arthropoda: insects, spiders, crabs. Jointed legs and a chitin shell. The largest phylum.
  • Echinodermata: starfish, spiny skin.

Think of each phylum as a different blueprint. Sponges filter water through pores, much as a sieve does. Cnidarians have two tissue layers and tentacles with stinging cells (cnidocytes). Flatworms are flat, with no body cavity, so every cell is near the surface. Roundworms have a gut with two openings, while earthworms are divided into repeated segments, and Indian earthworms improve soil. Molluscs have a muscular foot and often a shell; octopus and squid are clever molluscs. Arthropods shed their hard coat as they grow (moulting), and echinoderms move by water-filled tube feet.
All belong to phylum Chordata. Five classes:

At some stage, all chordates have a notochord, a hollow nerve cord above it, and gill slits. In vertebrates the notochord becomes the backbone. Warm-blooded animals (birds, mammals) keep a steady body temperature using energy; cold-blooded ones rely on the environment.

The chordate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Fish breathe with gills and have fins; amphibians, such as frogs, live partly on land and partly in water and have moist skin; reptiles have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs; birds have feathers and hollow bones; and mammals have hair and feed milk to their young. The terms 'warm-blooded' and 'cold-blooded' are better written as endotherm and ectotherm, and a snake basking in the sun is using its surroundings to warm up.

Insects have three body parts, six legs and often wings. Many go through metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult in butterflies). Bees, ants and termites live in complex societies. Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance (Nobel 1973).

A butterfly's change is called complete metamorphosis, in which the caterpillar eats and grows, then the pupa rebuilds the body, and the adult flies away to mate. A grasshopper has incomplete metamorphosis, with young nymphs that look like small adults. Insects breathe through tiny tubes called tracheae, not lungs, and the hard chitin skeleton must be shed to grow. Insects pollinate about three-quarters of food crops, and honeybees are crucial. In the waggle dance, the angle of the dance gives the direction relative to the Sun, and its length gives the distance.

Egg-laying mammals (monotremes: platypus), pouched mammals (marsupials: kangaroo) and placental mammals (most). Whales and bats show how a mammal can return to water or learn to fly.

Monotremes, such as the platypus and echidna, lay eggs yet feed their young with milk. Marsupials give birth to tiny young that finish growing in a pouch, and most live in Australia and the Americas. Placental mammals nourish the foetus through a placenta, and include rodents, bats, whales, elephants and primates. Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, and whales' ancestors walked on land, a story shown by fossils from Pakistan and India.

Linnaeus (1758) set the base. Cuvier grouped animals by body plan (1812). Today DNA sequences revise trees: for example, birds are living dinosaurs, and whales are close kin to hippos.

Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae gave every species a two-part Latin name and nested groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A useful memory aid is that closer relatives share more levels. Cuvier, who also helped found the study of extinction, showed that fossil animals were different from living ones. DNA evidence has shown that hippos are the closest living relatives of whales, and that birds belong inside the dinosaur group, since small feathered theropods gave rise to them.

Fix these

  • Spiders are not insects (eight legs, two body parts).
  • Whales and bats are mammals, not fish or birds.
  • A jellyfish or starfish is not a fish.

Also, a bat is not a bird: it has fur, gives birth to live young and feeds them milk, and its wing is a skin stretched over elongated finger bones. Whales breathe air through lungs and have to surface. Dolphins and sharks look alike through convergent evolution, where similar needs (fast swimming) shape different lineages into similar forms.

Remember too that 'worm' is not a group: flatworms, roundworms and earthworms belong to three different phyla.

India shelters tiger, Asian elephant, Asiatic lion (only in Gir, Gujarat), one-horned rhinoceros and the gharial. Project Tiger began in 1973 and India now has more than 3,000 tigers by the 2022 count (3,682 estimated). Project Cheetah (2022) reintroduced cheetahs from Namibia and South Africa. Salim Ali (1896-1987), the Birdman of India, wrote the Book of Indian Birds (1941). The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 protects species.

• Animals are grouped by body plan.
  • Arthropods are the largest phylum.
  • Five vertebrate classes: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.
  • Many species exist only in India's special habitats.

Think about it:

  1. Why can amphibians not live far from water?
  2. Why is warm-bloodedness both costly and useful?
